verdict.rationale: Svelte's docs say components are written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Script blocks hold plain JS or TS, styles are ordinary scoped CSS, and state is updated like any other variable with no state API to learn. Community reports back this up: a back-end developer found it the most accessible frontend option, and a React and Vue developer praised its fewer abstractions. The story's goal of minimal new concepts is only partly met, though: runes ($state, $derived, $effect), template blocks like {#if}, and the compiler's superset-of-JavaScript nature are framework-specific things to learn, and IDE support has suffered from it. Missing for 10: evidence that runes and template-block syntax don't add a meaningful learning burden, and clean standard-JS tooling/IDE parity.

support.subject: As a developer, I can write components using standard markup, styling, and language syntax I already know, minimizing new concepts to learn

citations.quote: write breathtakingly concise components that do minimal work in the browser, using languages you already know — HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
there is no API for interacting with state — `count` is just a number, rather than an object or a function, and you can update it like you would update any other variable.
CSS inside a `<style>` block will be scoped to that component.
A `<script>` block contains JavaScript (or TypeScript, when adding the `lang="ts"` attribute) that runs when a component instance is created.
